rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural patterns such as masājid and mafātīḥ resist further broken pluralization as endpoint patterns; as male names they take sound masculine plurals and as female names sound feminine plurals.
rows.anchor: أما ما لا يكسر فنحو مساجد ومفاتيح لا تقول إلا مساجدون ومفاتيحون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural patterns that already have broken plural forms can be broken again as names: examples include aʿdāl to aʿādīl and aqwāl to aqāwīl, alongside abyāt, anʿām, and ajriba.
rows.anchor: قالوا أقاويل في أقوال وأبابيت في أبيات وأناعيم في أنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A plural-derived name such as aʿbud can take both a diminutive and a broken plural, yielding al-aʿābid, because its pattern permits these processes like a singular.
rows.anchor: وكذلك لو سميت رجلا بأعبد جاز فيه الأعابد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A three-consonant plural pattern used as a name follows the broken plural expected of a singular with that form, since it can shift into singular-like patterns and diminutives.
rows.anchor: فإن كان عدة حروفه ثلاثة أحرف فهو يكسر على قياسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man named on the fuʿūl pattern may form faʿāʾil, since fuʿūl can also be singular and behaves like an existing plural pattern.
rows.anchor: ولو سميت رجلا بفعول جاز أن تكسره فتقول فعائل لأن فعولا قد يكون الواحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man named Jamāl on a pattern like singular jirāb takes the broken plural expected of a singular of that form.
rows.anchor: والفعال نحو جمال إن سميت بها رجلا لأنها على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamra used as a name has shifted from its original meaning and behaves like qaṣʿa, allowing tamār just as qaṣʿa allows qiṣāʿ.
rows.anchor: ولو سميت رجلا بتمرة لكانت كقصعة لأنها قد تحولت عن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gemination is heavy, so Arabic favors distinct consonants and assimilation into one tongue movement; when the final consonant is quiescent, Hijaz preserves the form while Tamim quiesces the first and vowels the second.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن التضعيف يثقل على ألسنتهم وأن اختلاف الحروف أخف عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form radd stays unassimilated in faʿala because quiescing the ending would still leave gemination, while the first radical is inherently quiescent.
rows.anchor: فإن قيل ما بالهم قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nouns longer than three letters follow doubled-consonant rules of four-letter verbs: shift a vowel onto a preceding quiescent consonant, retain an existing vowel, and leave preceding alif unchanged; afʿal forms assimilate too.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن كل شيء من الأسماء جاوز ثلاثة أحرف فإنه يجري مجرى الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A dual nūn can drop and therefore differs from the inseparable doubled consonant after alif; separated doubled consonants do not undergo the same alteration.
rows.anchor: ولا تجرى ما بعد الألف مجرى ما بعد الألف في يضربانني

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil analyzes ṣabb as faʿala, supported by ṣababtu and ṣabāba, parallel to qaniʿa and qanāʿa.
rows.anchor: زعم الخليل أنها فعل لأنك تقول صببت صبابة كما تقول قنعت قناعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forms such as ṭabb and khāf follow the three-letter verbal pattern; the lack of an unassimilated tabbab confirms that faʿal is assimilated.
rows.anchor: ومثله رجل طب وطبيب كما تقول قرح وقريح ومذل ومذيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Three-letter nominals distinguish themselves from verbal forms: weak-verb-like nouns can retain original forms, other nonverbs preserve doubled patterns, and some simplify, as in ʿamīma to ʿamm and thunā.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى أنهم أجروا فعلا اسما من التضعيف على الأصل

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some speakers preserve the unassimilated faʿil form, as in ḍafaf, because this pattern can be sound in the qult class.
rows.anchor: وقد قال قوم في فعل فأجروه على الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh prefers ḍaff and ḍafū al-ḥāl over the reported ḍafaf and ḍafafū.
rows.anchor: رجل ضف وقوم ضفوا الحال

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil explains mā aḥsana ʿAbd Allāh as an exclamation, conceptually like saying shayʾun aḥsana ʿAbd Allāh; that paraphrase is illustrative, not an utterance.
rows.anchor: زعم الخليل أنه بمنزلة قولك شئ أحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exclamative construction has fixed order and cannot be recast as mā yaḥsunu or another ordinary verb form; it uses one pattern because speakers do not conjugate it.
rows.anchor: أن تقدم عبد الله وتؤخر ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form can derive from roots such as ḥasuna, karuma, and aʿṭā yet behaves as a fixed nominal pattern, like lāta and mā; ajdal is likewise treated as a noun despite its verbal root.
rows.anchor: وبناؤه أبدا من فعل وفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In innī mimmā an aṣnaʿ, mā alone is a noun meaning the matter.
rows.anchor: قول العرب إنى مما أن أصنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naʿman in ghusiltuhu ghaslan naʿman means excellent washing, literally niʿma al-ghusl.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك غسلته غسلا نعما أى نعم الغسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding kāna in mā kāna aḥsana Zaydan marks the exclamation as referring to the past.
rows.anchor: وتقول ما كان أحسن زيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamzat al-waṣl is prefixed so speech can begin before a quiescent consonant; it is an added, vowelled onset.
rows.anchor: فلم تصل إلى أن تبتدئ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waṣl occurs in imperatives of form I when the next consonant is quiescent, in forms such as infaʿala, ifʿalla, and iftaʿala, and in five further derived patterns including istafʿala.
rows.anchor: من باب فعل يفعل ما لم يتحرك ما بعدها وذلك قولك اضرب اقتل اسمع اذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif in afʿala is formative rather than an added onset for a quiescent consonant, so its conjugation behaves like a four-letter verb.
rows.anchor: تلحق لأنهم أسكنوا الفاء ولكنها بني بها الكلمة وصارت فيها بمنزلة ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A waṣl alif drops after preceding speech because earlier words remove the need for an onset; Sībawayh compares this to dropping hāʾ in vocative speech.
rows.anchor: الألفات إذا كان قبلها كلام حذفت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the start of speech, waṣl is normally kasra but takes ḍamma when the third letter has ḍamma.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الألف الموصولة فيما ذكرنا في الابتداء مكسورة أبدا إلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites al-Nuʿmān b. Bashīr's line as a poetic example following the rule for adjusting vowels together.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك البيت للنعمان بن بشير الأنصاري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif-lām identifies nouns and behaves like qad or sawfa; Ghaylan's line uses bi-dhal and bi-jal, and Sībawayh says the lām is not broken once the form is complete.
rows.anchor: دع ذا وعجل ذا وألحقنا بذل

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil treats the article as separable like qad and sawfa but meaningful; its initial fatḥa distinguishes it, and it remains before an interrogative alif to distinguish question from statement.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل أنها مفصولة كقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's līman Allāh attests the connected onset in the oath expression.
rows.anchor: وقال فريق القوم لما نشدتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh reports Yunus's account that some speakers say īm Allāh with kasra, then līm Allāh by analogy with the waṣl in ibn.
rows.anchor: إيم الله فكسر ثم قال ليم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a man named Rād is addressed as yā Rād, kasra is restored because that is the vowel the consonant would have had without assimilation.
rows.anchor: وهو قولك في رجل اسمه راد يا راد أقبل وإنما كانت الكسرة أولى الحركات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In truncating Mufarr, the first rāʾ remains quiescent because its preceding consonant is vowelled.
rows.anchor: وأما مفر فإذا حذفت منه وهو اسم رجل لم تحرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truncated Muḥmār and Muḍārr retain the vowel of the original doubled form; the passive-intended Muḍārr is likewise treated as shortened from muḍārrar.
rows.anchor: وإن حذفت من اسم محمار أو مضار قلت يا محمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first rāʾ of a doubled form is not an ordinary augment and should not be deleted with the second; its behavior differs from genuine augment letters.
rows.anchor: هذا الحرف ليس من حروف الزيادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Asḥār loses its final rāʾ, the preceding quiescent rāʾ must be vowelled to avoid two adjacent quiescent consonants.
rows.anchor: فإنك إذا حذفت الراء الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fatḥa on Asḥār's rāʾ follows the nearest vowel source, like the vowel placed on the last consonant in jussive geminates.
rows.anchor: وحركته الفتحة لأنه يلي الحرف الذي منه الفتحة وهو الألف

rows.speaker: رجل من أزد السراة
rows.claim: A man of Azd al-Sarāt is cited reciting a line about a child and father, supporting the rule that the nearest vowel supplies the movement.
rows.anchor: وهو قول رجل من أزد السراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asḥār differs from Muḥmār: Muḥmār's underlying form has two rāʾs, while Asḥār is inherently assimilated and its first rāʾ is only quiescent.
rows.anchor: أن أصل محمار محمارر يدلك على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In coordinated clauses, the nearer verb governs the noun visibly, while the first predication remains understood; the listener recovers it without giving one noun both nominative and accusative roles.
rows.anchor: فالعامل في اللفظ أحد الفعلين وأما في المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites Qur'an 33:35 as evidence that a later coordinated form can leave unexpressed material already supplied by the earlier form.
rows.anchor: الحافظين فروجهم والحافظات والذاكرين الله كثيرا والذاكرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nearer governor is preferred for proximity and because the listener can recover the earlier predication; prepositional phrases show the same attachment principle.
rows.anchor: وكانت الباء أقرب إلى الاسم من الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qays b. al-Khaṭīm's coordinated نحن and أنت share the predicate rāḍ, illustrating understood material across clauses.
rows.anchor: نحن بما عندنا وأنت بما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍābiʾ al-Burjumī coordinates the speaker with Qiyār under a shared predicate, another poetic case of understood material.
rows.anchor: فمن يك أمسى بالمدين رحله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Aḥmar uses a singular predicate for himself and his father; the listener understands that the quality applies to both.
rows.anchor: رمانى بأمر كنت منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq omits a predicate after the first coordinated clause because the later predicate lets the listener recover it.
rows.anchor: إنى ضمنت لمن أتانى ما جنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred construction uses the nearer verb without putting a singular form for a plural, or a plural for a singular; poetry further illustrates the rule.
rows.anchor: والأول أجود لأنه لم يضع واحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With a first singular verb followed by a plural verb and a noun, the form is licensed either by the akalūnī al-barāghīth dialect or by apposition to the plural pronoun.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت ضربت وضربوني قومك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the following noun is the nearer verb's subject, an earlier verb still needs an understood subject; a verb may lack an object but cannot lack a subject.
rows.anchor: لأن الفعل قد يكون بغير مفعول ولا يكون الفعل بغير فاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ḍarabnī wa-ḍarabtuhum qawmuka, the noun can be raised by the nearer verb with an understood pronoun; apposition instead requires the plural ḍarabūnī.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت ضربنى وضربتهم قومك رفعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nominative noun after ḍarabtu wa-ḍarabnī is usual; accusative Zaydan is possible by analogy with expressions such as matā raʾayta Zaydan munṭaliqan.
rows.anchor: وقد يجوز ضربت وضربنى زيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍarabnī wa-ḍarabtu qawmuka is possible but awkward if treated as singular; special agreement such as huwa aḥsan al-fityān wa-ajmaluhu does not generalize to ordinary noun phrases.
rows.anchor: أن تجعل اللفظ كالواحد كما تقول

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash calls the singular-agreement analysis poor by analogy and warns it could wrongly license forms such as aṣḥābuka jalasa.
rows.anchor: فهذا ردئ في القياس يدخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq, Ṭufayl al-Ghanawī, and a poet of Bāhila illustrate clauses where the first verb is understood semantically while the second governs in form and meaning; their lines include سبني, جرى, and تصبى.
rows.anchor: وكمتا مدماة كأن متونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUmar b. Abī Rabīʿa illustrates an understood subject pronoun appearing in the latter clause of the coordinated construction.
rows.anchor: إذا هى لم تستك بعود أراكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Marrār al-Asadī's verse supplies another poetic example of the coordinated construction and its understood pronoun.
rows.anchor: فرد عل الفؤاد هوى عميدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays uses قليل as nominative because little money is not what he seeks; making it the object of طلب would distort the intended meaning.
rows.anchor: فلو أن ما أسعى لأدنى معيشة
